items.readable_text:
Content:
Imagine a ball is dropped from a [MATH: 78.4\,\text{m}] rooftop. How do we determine how long it will take for the ball to hit the ground?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/12e20a7b8dc44b5cee9061992a80eaef]

Content:
We can show that the distance traveled by a falling object can be modeled using the quadratic function
[MATH: s=ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2.]
This equation looks tricky, so let's go through each variable:

Content:
- [MATH: s] is the displacement of the object, measured in meters. For our purposes, the displacement measures the object's distance from the starting point.
- [MATH: u] is the initial velocity of the object, measured in meters per second.
- [MATH: t] is time, measured in seconds.
- [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2] is a constant known as the acceleration due to gravity. It tells us the acceleration of a falling object close to the earth's surface.

Content:
In our example, we want to find the time it takes for a ball to fall a distance of
[MATH: s =78.4\,\textrm{m}.]
Since the ball was dropped, its initial velocity was zero. Therefore, we have
[MATH: u = 0 \,\textrm{m/s}.]

Content:
Substituting the known values into our equation for [MATH: s] and solving for [MATH: t,] we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: 78.4|= (0)t + (1)/(2)(9.8)t^{2}; 78.4|= 4.9t^{2}; t^{2}|= (78.4)/(4.9); t^{2}|= 16; t|= ± 4]

Content:
So, we have two solutions, [MATH: t=4] and [MATH: t=-4] seconds. However, we are only interested in the positive solution because the ball hits the ground after some positive duration of time has passed.

Content:
Therefore, the ball will hit the ground after [MATH: t=4] seconds.

items.title: Solving for Displacement

sections.normalized_html: A penny is projected vertically downward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 300 \, \textrm{m/min}] and hits the ground after [MATH: 2] seconds. Find the distance the penny covered during its fall.
sections.readable_text: A penny is projected vertically downward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 300 \, \textrm{m/min}] and hits the ground after [MATH: 2] seconds. Find the distance the penny covered during its fall.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we use the formula [MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,] where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

  • We can find the initial velocity of the object in meters per second as follows: [MATH: u|= 300(m)/(min); = 300(m)/(min) ⋅ (min)/(60s); = 300(m)/(min) ⋅ (min)/(60s); = (300)/(60) ⋅ (m)/(s); = 5m/s]

  • The penny falls for [MATH: t=2\,\textrm{s}.]

  • The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = (5)(2) + (1)/(2)(9.8)(2)^{2}; = 10 + 19.6; = 29.6]

Therefore, the distance is [MATH: 29.6\,\textrm{m}.]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we use the formula [MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,] where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

  • The initial velocity of the stone is [MATH: u=14.7\,\textrm{m/s}.]

  • The stone covers the distance of [MATH: s=19.6\,\textrm{m}.]

  • The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: t,] we obtain the following:

[MATH: 19.6|= (14.7)t + (1)/(2)(9.8)t^{2}; 4(4.9)|= 3(4.9)t + (4.9)t^{2}; 4(4.9)|= 3(4.9)t + (4.9)t^{2}; 4|= 3t + t^{2}; t^{2} + 3t − 4|= 0; (t + 4)(t − 1)|= 0; t|= − 4, 1]

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the stone hits the ground after [MATH: t=1] second.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Imagine a ball is dropped from a [MATH: 78.4\,\text{m}] rooftop. How do we determine how long it will take for the ball to hit the ground?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/12e20a7b8dc44b5cee9061992a80eaef]

Content:
We can show that the distance traveled by a falling object can be modeled using the quadratic function
[MATH: s=ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2.]
This equation looks tricky, so let's go through each variable:

Content:
- [MATH: s] is the displacement of the object, measured in meters. For our purposes, the displacement measures the object's distance from the starting point.
- [MATH: u] is the initial velocity of the object, measured in meters per second.
- [MATH: t] is time, measured in seconds.
- [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2] is a constant known as the acceleration due to gravity. It tells us the acceleration of a falling object close to the earth's surface.

Content:
In our example, we want to find the time it takes for a ball to fall a distance of
[MATH: s =78.4\,\textrm{m}.]
Since the ball was dropped, its initial velocity was zero. Therefore, we have
[MATH: u = 0 \,\textrm{m/s}.]

Content:
Substituting the known values into our equation for [MATH: s] and solving for [MATH: t,] we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: 78.4|= (0)t + (1)/(2)(9.8)t^{2}; 78.4|= 4.9t^{2}; t^{2}|= (78.4)/(4.9); t^{2}|= 16; t|= ± 4]

Content:
So, we have two solutions, [MATH: t=4] and [MATH: t=-4] seconds. However, we are only interested in the positive solution because the ball hits the ground after some positive duration of time has passed.

Content:
Therefore, the ball will hit the ground after [MATH: t=4] seconds.

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving for Displacement

Example Prompt:
A penny is projected vertically downward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 300 \, \textrm{m/min}] and hits the ground after [MATH: 2] seconds. Find the distance the penny covered during its fall.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this problem, we use the formula
[MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,]
where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- We can find the initial velocity of the object in meters per second as follows:
[MATH: u|= 300(m)/(min); = 300(m)/(min) ⋅ (min)/(60s); = 300(m)/(min) ⋅ (min)/(60s); = (300)/(60) ⋅ (m)/(s); = 5m/s]
- The penny falls for [MATH: t=2\,\textrm{s}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = (5)(2) + (1)/(2)(9.8)(2)^{2}; = 10 + 19.6; = 29.6]

Therefore, the distance is [MATH: 29.6\,\textrm{m}.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this problem, we use the formula
[MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,]
where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The ball falls for [MATH: t=4\,\textrm{s}.]
- The ball covers the distance of [MATH: s=110.4\, \textrm{m}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: u,] we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; (110.4)|= u(4) + (1)/(2)(9.8)(4)^{2}; 110.4|= 4u + 78.4; 32|= 4u; u|= 8]

Therefore, the initial velocity of the ball was [MATH: u= 8 \, \textrm{m/s}.]

A stone is projected vertically downward from a height of [MATH: 19.6\,\textrm{m}] with a velocity of [MATH: 14.7\,\textrm{m/s}.] How long will it take for the stone to hit the ground?

Explanation:
To solve this problem, we use the formula
[MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,]
where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the stone is [MATH: u=14.7\,\textrm{m/s}.]
- The stone covers the distance of [MATH: s=19.6\,\textrm{m}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: t,] we obtain the following:

[MATH: 19.6|= (14.7)t + (1)/(2)(9.8)t^{2}; 4(4.9)|= 3(4.9)t + (4.9)t^{2}; 4(4.9)|= 3(4.9)t + (4.9)t^{2}; 4|= 3t + t^{2}; t^{2} + 3t − 4|= 0; (t + 4)(t − 1)|= 0; t|= − 4, 1]

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the stone hits the ground after [MATH: t=1] second.
